title: Workflow and State Manipulation
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Workflow and State Manipulation.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 17: Business Logic, Concurrency, and Workflow Security. It builds practical understanding of Workflow and State Manipulation with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Workflow and State Manipulation makes secure behavior repeatable across implementation, dependencies, configuration, and release. Enforce business invariants on the server inside atomic transactions or with database constraints, and test duplicates, retries, concurrency, and invalid state transitions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Workflow and State Manipulation can be understood through this sequence: Define invariant → Model concurrent retries → Commit atomically → Test duplicate + race. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 126.1 Multi-step operation sequencing; 126.2 Out-of-order requests; 126.3 Client-controlled hidden fields; 126.4 Repeated or skipped workflow steps; 126.5 Secure revalidation of transaction preconditions. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Enforce business invariants on the server inside atomic transactions or with database constraints, and test duplicates, retries, concurrency, and invalid state transitions.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Enforce business invariants on the server inside atomic transactions or with database constraints, and test duplicates, retries, concurrency, and invalid state transitions. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Workflow and State Manipulation”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Workflow and State Manipulation in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
